title: Camara reflects on 'very special' F1 weekend debut
excerpt:
Rafael Camara has reflected on a “very special” first taste of Formula 1 action with the Haas rookie making his debut at home earlier than expected.

Following confirmation earlier this week that Esteban Ocon would no longer compete for the US outfit for the rest of 2026, the 21-year-old Brazilian – who had already been signed to race for the team in 2027 – stepped up to race for Haas at this weekend’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

With plenty of eyes on him at his home event, Camara was positive about his first day behind the wheel – especially given it was a track he had never driven at before – as he recorded P18 and P16 finishes in FP1 and FP2 respectively.

“It’s been a very nice weekend, very special,” said Camara. “Going into FP1, it was getting a bit more emotional. You can see the crowd in front of you and everyone’s just so excited.

“Once you get in the car and start driving, you just focus on your own thing. It’s the normal thing you’ve been doing all your life.

"It’s been a very nice weekend, a lot of things going on, but so far I think it’s been a good two sessions. We’re able to learn a lot and just keep improving through the day.”

Camara also acknowledged the challenge of adapting to the current generation of F1 machinery. While he has completed TPC (Testing of Previous Car) tests with both Haas and Ferrari, today marked his first outing in a 2026 Formula 1 car.

“Once you get in the car, it’s a completely different thing,” he explained. “In a way, you get different feelings. It’s quite difficult to simulate the real car.

“There were a lot of things to learn, a lot to adapt [to], and to process. As for tomorrow, it will be good tonight to just sit back, realise everything, understand more things and put things in place for tomorrow.”

His first day of running, however, didn’t pass without incident with the Brazilian reprimanded over an impeding moment with Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc. With the Monegasque on a flying lap, he was forced to take evasive action towards the wall at Turn 15 as the inexperienced Camara moved across.

“While the typical penalty for impeding in a Free Practice session is a warning, in this instance, we are of the view that a reprimand is warranted,” read the stewards’ document as they cited the situation that had been created was “clearly dangerous”.

Asked about the incident, Haas’ Head Of Car Engineering, Hoagy Nidd explained: “He’s full throttle. He’s starting a lap. He can’t really move any further to the right in the end, but it’s just one of those things. He’s absolutely flat out at that point.”

title: Red Bull ‘looking into quite a few changes’ for Verstappen
excerpt:
Red Bull are planning to make “quite a few changes” to Max Verstappen’s car ahead of Qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix after he suffered issues with the clutch and steering during Free Practice.

Although the Dutchman finished third in both FP1 and FP2, it wasn’t the smoothest day for him as he continued to struggle with his downshifts, which has been a recurring problem this season.

He also reported heavy steering on the RB22, referring to it as a “workout”, and ultimately ended the second session slightly early because of it.

Asked whether Red Bull had resolved the steering troubles, Head of Race Strategy Hannah Schmitz responded: “I think we’ll have a different wheel for the rest of the weekend, and we’re looking into quite a few changes on Max’s side.

“There are a number of things that he was unhappy with, but we know what they all are, and they’re all things that we can work on and improve.”

Verstappen has previously explained that he relays such concerns in order to “make sure that the team is always looking into details to try and find more lap time”, which Schmitz admitted does help to unlock extra performance.

“I think there is a lot of performance to gain, and obviously, in terms of lap times, we’re still pretty competitive up there with everybody else,” she said. “So, given there’s still quite a lot of potential in the car, that looks optimistic for the rest of the weekend.

“I think it was a useful day. There’s definitely a lot of things to work on and look into overnight, but in a way, that’s what practice is for. I think there’s a lot of potential in the car, so looking forward to the rest of the weekend.”

However, she did note that the unpredictable weather at Interlagos could influence Saturday’s Qualifying hour, with rain currently forecast in the afternoon.

“It looks like it’s a very heavy rain front,” she summarised. “So whether Qualifying will actually happen at the scheduled time, I guess, is what we will find out a bit more about tomorrow.

“There are a few forecasts where it looks like it might come just after Qualifying, so there is a chance of a dry Qualifying still. We’ll be prepared for all eventualities.”

While Verstappen found himself in a tight battle with Lando Norris and George Russell in FP2 – only 0.020s separated the trio as they occupied P2 to P4 – his team mate Isack Hadjar found himself over a second adrift of the benchmark set by Kimi Antonelli.

“I was not very happy,” the Frenchman said. “I thought there was free lap time in the balance. We went in one direction and it didn't work. So, work in progress. In the end, I feel like tomorrow anyway it's going to be raining.

“But still, I want to go into FP3 and be like, okay, solved something at least. On the long run, it seems competitive.

“This morning was competitive. It's just that one-lap, single-lap pace on the soft. We need to find some easy lap time, but we know where we're heading.”

title: What the teams said – Friday in Brazil
excerpt:
What the teams said – Friday in Brazil

The drivers and teams report back from Friday practice at the Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix in Brazil.

Nov 06, 2026 10:35pm UTC

Mercedes

Antonelli took to the track for the first time as a World Champion in FP1, and it looked like he was happy to pick up where he left off in Mexico with a strong performance. He was up there on both the medium and soft tyres, winding up less than a tenth off the pace. He went even better in the second session, topping the timing sheet by a handsome margin. On a day where the time gaps were small, his 0.253s lead over the field was impressive.

Russell has a five-place grid drop coming for Sunday after taking on a new ICE, but ran a standard programme as he looks to try and negate that penalty as much as possible. He could not match his team mate, but was very much in the mix just behind.

Kimi Antonelli - FP1: 1:11.799, P2; FP2: 1:10.763, P1

"It was a positive day overall and I felt good in the car, particularly on the single lap runs. The conditions were quite tricky with the low grip, and it wasn’t easy to find the right balance, but I think we made some good progress between FP1 and FP2. There is still more to improve with both the car and my driving, so we’ll work through everything tonight and see what we can find for tomorrow.

"It looks very close at the front. McLaren and Red Bull look strong, and we know Ferrari can often find something extra when we get to qualifying, so I expect it to be a really tight fight. The weather could also play a part. It’s very difficult to predict at the moment, so we need to be ready for anything and react quickly if the conditions change.

"After the highs of Mexico, I’m just focusing on each session as it comes this weekend but I am enjoying things so far. Hopefully we can take another step tomorrow and put ourselves in a good position for qualifying and continue that feeling."

George Russell - FP1: 1:12.103, P5; FP2: 1:11.036, P4

"Overall, it was a solid Friday. We look to be in the mix, although it’s very close between several teams at the front. The long run pace felt stronger than our single-lap performance on my side, so there are definitely areas we can work on overnight to try and find a bit more ahead of Qualifying. The car wasn't perfect and we've got some understeer to dial out; there’s still some performance to find if we want to be fighting right at the front tomorrow.

"The conditions are likely to change across the weekend, so what we saw today won’t necessarily be fully representative of what we face tomorrow and Sunday. It looks like we’re in for another really close fight and small margins are going to make a difference.

"Obviously, the five-place grid penalty we have makes our task a little more difficult. It puts even more emphasis on having a strong qualifying and putting the car as high up the grid as possible before the penalty is applied. If we can do that, then I’m confident we can still put ourselves in a position to move forward and challenge near the front on Sunday."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"This has been one of our better Fridays recently from a pace point of view, although there is still plenty of scope to improve the balance. FP1 was interesting as Kimi looked very comfortable on the single lap but struggled a little more on the long run, whereas George was very strong on the long run but didn’t quite get the single lap together. That gave us some useful data ahead of the afternoon and we were able to take the best elements from each set-up into FP2.

"The second session ran smoothly and, overall, we look to have decent pace on both the single lap and long run. There is still work to do though, and both drivers are finding the cars difficult in certain areas. Brake locking is one of those and has been a bit of a theme for us over the past few races. We’d also like to find a better compromise between rear grip through the high-speed corners and giving the drivers the strong front end they need in the slower sections. Whilst the pace is encouraging then, we’ve still got plenty to work on overnight. If we can make the cars a little easier for the drivers to work with and tidy up those areas of balance, hopefully we can take another step forward tomorrow."

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy driving the (12) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

McLaren

Norris wound up fastest in FP1 by 0.082s from Antonelli, the McLaren man setting his lap time a few moments after the Italian and thus on a slightly more evolved track. Nonetheless it was a strong lap and showed McLaren could be in the mix here. Fornaroli also had a decent session, finishing 11th after running the soft tyre first before the track had rubbered in.

Piastri took his cockpit back in FP2, and both McLaren drivers found themselves evenly matched. Norris had the edge, but only by 0.068s.

Lando Norris - FP1: 1:11.717, P1; FP2: 1:11.016, P2

"It’s been a positive day. FP1 was a pleasant surprise, and although we found FP2 slightly more challenging compared to Mercedes, our pace relative to the rest of the field looked strong. We’ve been working through the upgrades, and the first signs are encouraging: we seem to have gained performance and a little lap time.

"The upgrades are designed to bring more load and grip, rather than alter the car’s handling, but they can still affect how the car feels. The car has been tricky this year, but today it felt a little more straightforward and positive, which is a good start to the weekend. We’ll analyse everything carefully and make sure we do our best to prepare, particularly with very wet conditions expected on Saturday."

Oscar Piastri - FP2: 1:11.084, P5

"A reasonable session to start the weekend. Everything feels good and the upgrades look positive, which is encouraging. We’ll now keep building on that to put ourselves in the best window for Qualifying tomorrow afternoon.

"There’s still a bit of work to do to catch the cars ahead, but overall, I think it was a pretty successful first day. Thanks to Leo for his efforts in FP1 and the useful work he did for the team. We’ve got plenty to look through tonight, and hopefully we can take another step forward in the remaining sessions."

Leonardo Fornaroli - FP1: 1:12.833, P11

"It was a positive FP1 session today, this was my first time at the circuit and I really enjoyed it. There was a lot to get through, particularly with the aerodynamic work at the start but I’m pleased with the progress we’ve made since Mexico. The car felt good, and I’m happy with all the work we completed today.

"Once more, thank you to the Zak, Andrea and the rest of the team for the opportunity and all their support this season. This was my final FP1 session of the year, but I’ll keep working in the simulator and supporting the team as Reserve Driver for the remaining races of the season."

Randy Singh - Senior Director, Racing

"It has been an encouraging day for the team. We brought a new upgrade package, including a revised front wing, and the data from both practice sessions indicates that it is delivering exactly as anticipated. Both drivers were immediately competitive, with Oscar doing a fantastic job to hit the pace straight away in FP2 despite sitting out the opening session in tricky, misty conditions. Leo too did a very good job in FP1, helping the team to collect very important data but also being able to show his natural speed, despite he had to run on a set of used Softs when he had the possibility to properly push for the lap time.

"The car feels like it has taken a small step forward compared to recent events, putting us in a much stronger position to compete near the front. Looking ahead to qualifying, the margins remain extremely fine across the field; a good session could easily be the difference between the front row and starting seventh or eighth. We will complete our due diligence on the data tonight before confirming our setup for the remainder of the weekend."

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Lando Norris of Great Britain driving the (1) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Oscar Piastri of Australia and McLaren prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Hector Vivas - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Leonardo Fornaroli of Italy and McLaren prepares to drive during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

Red Bull

Verstappen was his usual vocal self on the radio in FP1, complaining about downshifts and also his steering wheel. Despite claiming that driving had turned into a “workout,” the Dutchman finished in the top three, a few places higher than Hadjar. He had similar issues in the second session and wound up parking in the garage earlier than planned, with the team needing to look at his steering wheel. But he was quick throughout the day, and looks right in the mix for pole. Hadjar has a little bit more work to do, he wound up down in ninth after being the first to bolt on the soft tyres.

Max Verstappen - FP1: 1:11.953, P3; FP2: 1:11.022, P3

“The session went fairly well today. We’re always looking to extract a little more performance, while also trying to find more consistency in our overall performance. We’ve been fine-tuning the car and, in particular, working to better understand the tyre behaviour over the long runs. I had some issues with the steering, which we’ll need to fix ahead of qualifying. There’s still a bit of work to do, but nothing major. We’ll focus on maximising our performance and maybe hope for a little bit of rain."

Isack Hadjar - FP1: 1:12.156, P6; FP2: 1:11.839, P9

“We had a pretty consistent day today and were competitive on the long runs this morning, although we’re still working on finding the right balance. FP2 was more challenging as we went in a different direction with the setup, which didn’t quite work out as expected. We know where we need to improve and will make some adjustments ahead of tomorrow. It looks like we could have some rain, so we’ll need to adapt to the conditions, but hopefully we can make another step forward with the car.”

Hannah Schmitz, Head of Race Strategy

“It was a useful day. There was definitely a lot of things to work on and look into, but that is what practice is for. It was a close call on which session we would run the Hard and which session we would run the Medium tyres. Ultimately most of the top teams tested the three compounds, as they are so similar, but what we will run comes down to driver and Team preference.

"For both Max and Isack, there are things they want to look into and change overnight. There is a lot of performance that we can extract, and, in terms of lap times, we are still very competitive up there with the rest of the field. The Team are looking into several changes for Max’s car. There were things he was unhappy with, but we know what they are so can work on them.

"Tomorrow, the forecast is looking wet and we will have to wait and see if Qualifying happens at the scheduled time, but we will be prepared for all eventualities.”

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands and Oracle Red Bull Racing prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Isack Hadjar of France driving the (6) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains in the Pitlane during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

Ferrari

Beganovic was in for Leclerc in the opening session, but he did not have much chance to impress with reliability issues limiting him to just 11 laps. He did not manage to get a flying lap in on the softs, but at least Leclerc had Hamilton’s data to look through.

Hamilton had a decent first hour, but both Ferrari drivers found the second session more difficult. Neither could nail that flying lap, with Leclerc also impeded by Camara on one of his runs – something that left the Monegasque driver less than impressed on the radio.

Charles Leclerc - FP2: 1:11.483, P7

"I only drove in FP2 today and it was quite a tricky session. The feeling in the car wasn’t quite right, so there’s plenty for us to work on tonight. I have some ideas about the direction we need to take with the set-up and we’ll make some changes for tomorrow. We need to find some performance, and hopefully we can make a good step forward for qualifying."

Lewis Hamilton - FP1: 1:12.041, P4; FP2: 1:11.213, P6

"It was a challenging day. The track is very bumpy and slippery, which made it difficult to get the tyres into the right window. FP1 was okay overall, but FP2 proved more difficult. We’ve gathered plenty of useful data, so we’ll work through that with the team tonight to understand where we can improve the car ahead of qualifying tomorrow."

Dino Beganovic - FP1: 1:14.357, P21

"It was great to be back in the car and experience such an amazing track behind the wheel. The first part of the session went well, and we collected some interesting data, however, unfortunately, our session was cut short by an issue and we didn’t manage to put in as many laps as we planned.

"It’s always special to drive the SF26, and to be part of the team, and I’m thankful for the opportunity to run the car in a free practice. I hope to be back in the car soon."

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain driving the (44) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Charles Leclerc of Monaco and Scuderia Ferrari prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Hector Vivas - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Dino Beganovic of Sweden driving the (38) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Buda Mendes/Getty Images)

Audi

Slater was in for Hulkenberg in the opening session, but his participation did not last long as he was forced to park up trackside with an issue. That led to a red flag stoppage, which was a shame for the rookie who was robbed of the chance to show what he is made of.

Bortoleto at least had a clean opening hour on home soil and finished in the top 10. It was much of the same for the Brazilian in FP2, as he tries to build a less incident-packed weekend than he managed last year. Hulkenberg, however, was left without a single lap on the opening day, the issue with his car preventing him from going out at all in FP2.

Nico Hulkenberg - FP2: No time set, P22

“No laps for me today. Following the issue Freddie had in FP1, the team managed to identify the problem and worked hard to fix it but, unfortunately, we ran out of time to get me out on track in FP2. I followed Gabi's session alongside the engineers, and we'll go through the data he collected. Not an easy day, but we'll try to recover and make the most of FP3 tomorrow.”

Gabriel Bortoleto - FP1: 1:12.614, P8; FP2: 1:11.780, P8

“It's been an encouraging first day overall. We had a good start to the weekend and went through all of our task-list for the day; the car felt very good out there, and that also helped me getting the most out of it. Hopefully, we can keep this energy going through the rest of the weekend.”

Freddie Slater- FP1: 1:14.966, P22

“Of course, missing a session is frustrating as a driver because you just want to drive, that's what we love to do, but I know that's part of motorsport and these things can happen. On the other hand, the laps I did were positive. On the hard tire I got some good, valuable lessons, so I’ll take that with me and move on. It's been an amazing experience over these two weekends and I am grateful to Audi Revolut F1 Team for it. I've learned so much already, both from the team and about how these cars work, and it's been a great opportunity to gain valuable experience that will help me in the future.”

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Gabriel Bortoleto of Brazil driving the (5) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Alex Bierens de Haan/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Freddie Slater of Great Britain driving the (98) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Alex Bierens de Haan/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Nico Hulkenberg of Germany and Audi F1 Team looks on from the fan stage prior to practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Hector Vivas - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Alpine

Gasly sat out for Mini in FP1, and the rookie did a very good job, topping the midfield and beating his team mate. He wound up nearly a tenth ahead of Colapinto, but the Argentine still had a solid day. He was on the cusp of the top 10 in the second session, just 0.005s behind Bearman. As for Gasly, he took a little longer to get going after returning for FP2, so it remains to be seen if he can climb up the order tomorrow at a track where he has a very decent record.

Pierre Gasly - FP2: 1:12.109, P14

“A slightly different Friday to normal for me today with Gabriele [Mini] in my car for Free Practice 1, so only the one session in the car on my side during Free Practice 2. Gabriele did a great job in that session to be up in P7, and it appeared the car was quite well balanced from the very start with Franco also up inside the top 10. I do not think the leaderboard in Free Practice 2 reflects how I am feeling inside the car after that session. While I am not completely happy with a few things, it was a bit messy our end on the Soft tyre and I locked up on my first push lap and then had to abort another, so there is definitely much more performance to quickly unlock and show. I am definitely feeling optimistic, especially as a tenth of a second makes up four places or so. I have always enjoyed driving at this track, so I am looking forward to more Practice tomorrow ahead of Qualifying where we'll give it our all to be in Q3 again.”

Franco Colapinto - FP1: 1:12.654, P9; FP2: 1:11.996, P11

“It is good to be back in São Paulo and driving in Interlagos, this legendary track, always feels so special. Today went quite well and, in terms of competitiveness, we are looking quite good. We have some more work to do on the balance of the car and trying to feel more comfortable, but the team and I will work hard tonight to go through the data to see what areas we can change and improve. The underlying pace is there and the gaps to some of our rivals are very close, so it is important to maximise every detail. The track here has been resurfaced and it feels okay in the dry, some of the usual bumps remain, but, of course, we have not yet driven in wet conditions. There is some rain forecast, so that is something for us all to keep an eye on.”

Gabriele Mini - FP1: 1:12.569, P7

“I am quite happy with how my second Free Practice session with the team went and, obviously, finishing in P7 was a pretty good result. I learnt a lot of things last weekend in Mexico City, so I knew a few areas I needed to work on heading into today, which was very useful. I began the programme with some aero testing which is important for the team with the useful data it provides. After that we moved into some performance running, starting on Mediums and then onto Softs. I felt the car was in a good place and I was relatively pleased with my push lap on Softs. There was definitely more time in that lap but there is also a lot to manage inside the car, so I also know it was far from perfect. Still, I was able to show some pace which was good, I was happy with it, and it was satisfying to learn that I was amongst the quickest of everyone in some corners on the lap. It was very different to Mexico, I felt way more grip here and I was just building and improving lap after lap. Once again, thank you to the team for the opportunity and now I look forward to seeing what I can do to assist the team for the remainder of the weekend.”

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Franco Colapinto of Argentina driving the (43) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes leaves the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Pierre Gasly of France driving the (10) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Gabriele Mini of Italy driving the (62) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Alex Bierens de Haan/Getty Images)

Haas

Camara had a solid opening session for Haas, getting plenty of laps in and setting a strong foundation for his weekend. Bearman was 12th in FP1, despite locking up his tyres early in the session.

Bearman improved on that in the second hour of practice, winding up in the top 10 which bodes well for Qualifying. Camara found the second session more testing, after drifting across onto the racing line with a flying Leclerc coming up behind. That led to a hairy moment, which the stewards had a look at after the session, giving the rookie a reprimand.

Oliver Bearman - FP1: 1:12.837, P12; FP2: 1:11.991, P10

“It was a decent day and I was happy with the car. Sometimes it was a bit more challenging than others, but we found a decent baseline. I’m proud of the guys and we’ll keep working overnight to find a bit more to see what we can do in Qualifying – not knowing what weather conditions we may be running in.”

Rafael Camara - FP1: 1:13.696, P18; FP2: 1:12.561, P16

“It’s been a really nice weekend so far, really special. Going into FP1 was getting a bit more emotional, with the intensity of the crowd in front of you and fans getting excited. Once you get into the car, and you start driving, it goes back to the normal thing that you’ve been doing your whole life. There’s a lot going on, but so far it’s been a good two sessions, learning a lot and improving throughout the day. Tonight, I’ll work with the team and put more in place for tomorrow.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“Overall, it’s been a decent Friday. It’s the first day for our debutant Rafa in his home country, so there was a lot going on, but he and the team have handled the situation very well. He’s very calm with a professional approach, and had two solid sessions, so I’m very pleased with that and think we’ve got off to a good start. On Ollie’s side, in FP1 he wasn’t as happy with the car as he had been previously, but we’ve actually got a pretty decent reference from other races, and in FP2 he was happier, especially on the softs. We really couldn’t get the hard tyres working, so that’s something we’ve got to look into. On quali runs, because of the difference in hards and softs, we left some performance out there. I think the baseline is good, and it’s now at the fine-tuning stage of understanding what we can do better on the medium and hard compounds, and at the same time, getting a bit more out of the soft tyre.”

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Oliver Bearman of Great Britain driving the (87) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Rafael Camara of Brazil driving the (51) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Alex Pantling/Getty Images)

Racing Bulls

Lawson rounded out the top 10 in first practice in what was a steady session for him. Lindblad was further back and took avoiding action via an escape road at one point, keen not to tangle with Verstappen on track like his team mate did in Mexico. But the rookie beat Lawson in the second session, albeit on a day where the gaps were as tight in the midfield as they were up front. title: ‘Ferrari comes first’ – Vasseur confirms Hamilton/Leclerc talks
excerpt:
Ferrari Team Principal Fred Vasseur has insisted he is not asking Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to be “best friends” after holding talks with the pair following their on-track battle at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The Scuderia drivers went wheel-to-wheel during the opening lap at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, with the team ultimately missing out on a potential one-two finish after Leclerc received a five-second penalty for the incident involving his team mate Hamilton.

The Briton called for discussions over the rules of engagement between drivers ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with Vasseur confirming during Friday’s Team Representatives’ press conference that a meeting had taken place the previous evening.

“We spoke yesterday evening because I had to fly back to Europe between the two races," Vasseur explained.

"It went well. It was good to discuss things and clarify my position and their positions. Now we turn the page and focus on the next one.

"I think they've accumulated a bit of frustration because they're starting each weekend side by side, and you have an accumulation of incidents. At the end of the day, the guidelines are always the same. They need to respect each other. They're two competitors with a fighting spirit, but they need to respect one another.

“Mainly, and firstly, they need to respect the brand, the team, the people working at home and the people working at the track. We're putting a lot of effort into this, and the message was clear and will stay clear."

Vasseur also made clear that Ferrari's interests must remain the priority, acknowledging that the team had collectively fallen short after failing to convert its strong position in Mexico City into victory.

“We failed collectively because we were one-two and didn't win the race in the end," the Ferrari boss added. "The conclusion of the meeting yesterday evening was clear. It was a reminder that Ferrari comes first, for the brand, for the employees and for the Tifosi."

Asked whether managing Hamilton and Leclerc was proving particularly challenging, Vasseur pointed to Ferrari’s recent form and the benefits of having two closely-matched drivers, despite the potential for tensions to rise.

"For sure, we have two experienced, competitive guys," he said.

"It's now four or five races in a row that we've been at the front, scoring the highest number of points after Monza and Madrid. You have an escalation because they both want to win races. I think that's probably the downside of the system. We have two competitive guys starting each weekend next to each other.

"But we are P2 today, because we have two guys who are very close, and we have to manage it. It's a choice in the line-up, and has positives and negatives. But I will deal with the negatives."

Vasseur was also questioned about the relationship between Hamilton and Leclerc, and whether he was concerned by Hamilton’s insistence that he would not be silenced following the events in Mexico.

"I was clear with Lewis, and I'll keep that between Lewis and myself," he responded.

"You can't compare the relationship between Carlos [Sainz] and Charles, Charles and Lewis, or Lewis and Valtteri [Bottas] in the past. They have different personalities.

"I'm not asking them to be best friends. I think that would probably even be a bit negative. I'm just asking them to act and work as professionals, and that's it."

The Frenchman further emphasised the importance of putting Ferrari’s employees first when pressed on whether consequences had been established should similar incidents occur in the future.

"We had a discussion, and it has to stay private. It's a matter of respect for them and for the team," he said.

"We're working for a brand, for sponsors, but mainly for the employees of the team. We've had a good recovery in terms of performance. We came back after Madrid in much better shape, and that's due to the work of the people at home. As a team, we all have to keep this in mind. It's not due to the wind. It's due to the work of the employees of the company."

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff also weighed in on the situation, drawing parallels with the infamous rivalry between Hamilton and Nico Rosberg during their time together at the Silver Arrows.

"It's like déjà vu because you asked me exactly the same questions for so many years, and then Nico called it a day," Wolff said.

"Sometimes, when you put two strong drivers in, the best ones have edges and they want to win. That's a situation that's always very difficult to cope with, particularly under the media spotlight when those cars are racing at the front. I can relate to what Fred is going through at the moment.

"Sometimes it needs a really tough incident to make a point. When I was there with Nico and Lewis, whenever there was an accident, it was understood that this was the limit and it wouldn't continue like that.

"It's about respect for the team – the many thousands of people and the brand they work for. That's what they need to keep in their heads."

title: Komatsu on why fast-tracking Camara was a ‘tough decision’
excerpt:
Haas Team Principal Ayao Komatsu has conceded that promoting Rafael Camara into the squad earlier than expected at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix was a "tough decision", in light of Ryo Hirakawa's solid performance one week earlier in Mexico City.

Camara’s Formula 1 debut at his home race at Interlagos is one of the biggest stories of a busy Sao Paulo GP weekend. The Brazilian had been due to make his first FP1 appearance in a current car with Ferrari, which would have been a useful step towards his planned Haas race debut next season.

However, the sudden departure of Esteban Ocon created an opportunity for the team to fast-track his race debut, accelerating his progress even further.

It might seem the obvious choice to make. However, Komatsu insists that it was not quite that straightforward, especially as Hirakawa did so well when he was called upon in Mexico City, ultimately claiming P10.

The Japanese driver already had a commitment at the Monza World Endurance Championship race for the Interlagos weekend, but it wasn’t necessarily a given that he raced in Italy rather than Brazil.

“It was a tough decision,” Komatsu said on Friday. “Ryo did a fantastic job in Mexico, with such short notice. Yes, he had FP1, but to then jump in the car from FP3 on, to deliver Qualifying, deliver the race, is a huge pressure, huge challenge.

“He's so professional, he's very, very good to work with. And again, his preparation, for somebody to be preparing for that long time, without knowing when that opportunity might arise, it's not easy. You've always got to be ready to perform at your best. But again, full credit to his professionalism. He's been preparing, so when that news was delivered, he was ready, and then he performed.

“So that of course makes my decision difficult here. It was definitely not an easy decision. Maybe from the outside, with who we signed next year, etcetera, it might look like a very easy decision. But it wasn't.”

While giving Camara a head start ahead of 2027 has obvious benefits, there are also potential pitfalls in terms of throwing him in at the deep end with minimal preparation, especially with the added attention that comes with racing in Brazil.

However, when making the call Komatsu was confident that the youngster could cope, especially having seen how he dealt with the Portimao TPC (Testing of Previous Cars) test 'shoot-out' that ultimately won him the 2027 race seat.

Camara looking to learn from Bearman on surprise F1 debut

“There's always pros and cons,” said Komatsu. “It's not a foregone thing that we signed him next year, let's put him as early as possible. There's always a risk.

“Of course, I don't know Rafa for many years, but what I saw in Portimao when we did a shoot-out, how he handled himself, how he contained all that pressure, how he created the environment that let him focus and perform, just everything around it, other than the pure lap time he did, which was impressive. Everything around it for me was very impressive, and such a mature approach.

“So that gave me obviously more confidence that, right, if we go in together [the] message is clear [and] our objective is clear. We can manage.

“If he was somebody who doesn't understand what the professional performing environment should be, if he was somebody that gets really overwhelmed by certain things, or excited by certain things, I would have maybe not have taken this decision. But from everything I saw in Portimao, it was positive, considering this circumstance.”

Komatsu’s views were bolstered by a series of calls with Camara during which those pros and cons were obviously discussed – and the team boss clearly liked what he heard.

“I spoke with Rafa on Sunday night, Monday, Tuesday,” he explained. “All the conversations just reinforced my belief what Rafa can, let's say, not even deliver, but how he can behave or deal with everything, and then shut the noise out. Focus, simplify, and also, not overcomplicate it.

“Again, what I saw in Portimao – conditions were changing all the time, so it was very, very difficult. And then of course, it was huge pressure for him. That was an F1 drive hanging there. But he didn't focus on that result, he didn't focus that I need to produce something to get an F1 drive. He didn't focus on that.

“He really focused on what he's good at, which is the natural, amazing feel he's got, listen to his feel, drive to the conditions. And the conditions honestly lap-by-lap were changing.

“He calmly from the outside did that, managed that mental side, managed that pressure side, not to chase something that is out of your control, just to focus on what you can deliver.

“That was impressive, and if we can take the same mindset here, that's what I believe we can. That's why I made that decision in the end.”

Officially Camara has only been confirmed for Interlagos, with the team yet to confirm their plans for the remaining races of the season.

The obvious catch is that he also has F2 commitments in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and abandoning the series – and therefore not securing the title – would be a difficult call. Komatsu insists that no decision has been made.

Bearman doesn't see Camara's debut 'as a shoot-out'

“I'd just like to take it one step at a time, really,” he said. “Because again for Rafael, it's a huge challenge. I really want to protect him, and I just don't want to put any external pressure.

“Of course, a complication is he's got the F2 championship as well. In a way I only, let's say, dealt with something I had to deal with, which is this weekend. So that's what we've done.

“And then we really focused on this weekend. It's a huge, huge debut weekend in front of his home crowd. So we really need to manage expectations and clear message, simplify everything, let him focus on what he's brilliant at doing.

“And then that's what we are focusing at this minute. So we just didn't want to get into any other conversation.”

title: Liam Lawson explains major Racing Bulls dilemma after failed Brazil experiment
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has explained the dilemma his Racing Bulls team face with its Sao Paulo Grand Prix set-up as rain is forecast to hit Interlagos.

Lawson finished the first session on Friday in 10th place, but slipped back to 13th in FP2, behind team-mate Arvid Lindblad as the team experimented with a set-up direction on the VCARB03 machine, which ultimately proved fruitless, as it induced too much understeer.

However, with rain forecast to hit Brazil for Sunday's race, drivers must carry the set-up they use in qualifying into the race, meaning what set-up might be best for the dry conditions of FP3 and qualifying, as currently forecast, would not translate into the race.

Reflecting on his day, Lawson explained the dilemma.

"We started a little bit stronger this morning, and then we tried something that didn't really work in FP2, and when it got a lot colder, the stuff we changed was in the opposite direction to that, so it didn't really help," Lawson explained.

"We'll probably go back on that. I think we had a better car [in FP1], so we'll try to start with something similar [in FP3], and then we'll see what happens with the weather because it is probably going to rain."

Looking ahead to qualifying, Lawson spoke of how tough it was to prepare the tyres for a lap, given the cold temperatures.

"Putting the lap together and basically doing a good job, I think it's very, very tough here," he said.

"For the tyres, the laps are really short for warm-up, so we're struggling to get everything properly ready for Turn 1.

"Any traffic queuing in the pit lane on track can really, really affect Turn 1, so it's going to be interesting, especially Q1 when everybody's on track together.

"But I mean, the bigger question mark is going to be the rain."

[Article continues below]

Lawson reflects on Friday

Then, when asked if the FP1 balance before the failed FP2 changes, would translate into a strong foundation, Lawson agreed.

"I think we're pretty surprised by how much of an effect what we changed had because the car was probably one of the worst balances we've had this season, or at least in the recent races in FP2," he said.

"But a big factor is that when the track temperature comes down, we just had so much understeer in the car, so we'll try and revert on that [for Saturday].

"But obviously, we can't change anything drastically because if it rains, you need to have a good car in the rain as well."

title: Lando Norris delivers verdict on latest McLaren upgrade ahead of Sao Paulo GP
excerpt:
Lando Norris has offered a cautiously positive assessment of McLaren's upgrade package introduced for this weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix.

McLaren is the only team to have brought updates to Interlagos, fitting a revised floor, a new beam wing, a reworked rear wing and a test-concept front wing, aimed at generating downforce more efficiently without adding excessive drag.

The timing of the package is notable given McLaren's struggles with the MCL40's narrow operating window this season, a trait traced back to a shorter wheelbase forced on the car early in its design to hit minimum weight targets.

That decision is reported to have permanently capped the floor's aerodynamic ceiling for 2026.

Norris, closing in on his time as F1 champion this year, has stressed that the upgrades have not been introduced purely to tame a car's behaviour.

Asked whether he could feel a step in improvement following Friday practice in which he finished second quickest behind the driver who will replace him as champion, Kimi Antonelli, speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Norris said: "It's tricky to say. You're always kind of pushing things to the limit.

"As soon as you feel something maybe a little bit more comfortable, you automatically push it until you find the limit again.

"Ultimately, the upgrades are there to bring lap time and performance. They're not set out to improve handling.

"A perfect upgrade brings lap time, and at the same time brings a handling upgrade, especially with how tricky the car's been.

"I would say maybe there's a small change in the right direction that it seems just a little bit more straightforward to drive.

"But I don't think we can ever judge things over just one track, but so far, things have seemed a little bit more straightforward, which is a good thing."

[Article continues below]

Norris - 'A pleasant surprise'

Asked whether Friday practice in São Paulo had been encouraging, Norris, who was quickest in FP1 by 0.082s ahead of Antonelli, but a quarter of a second adrift in FP2, pointed to a mixed but ultimately promising picture across the two sessions.

"I would say so. Certainly, FP1 was a little bit of a surprise, a pleasant surprise," he said.

"FP2, we seemed to struggle a little bit more compared to the Mercedes, [they were] two-tenths up on every lap, basically. But relative to some of the others, we seemed pretty good.

"The upgrades, even though I had half and then half, and we'll kind of put everything together for tomorrow, seem to have given what we hoped for, I would say.

"So I think it's been a good day in terms of getting through the run plan, and also a good day for relative performance."

title: F1 rookie learns stewards fate after 'clearly dangerous' Charles Leclerc incident
excerpt:
F1 rookie Rafael Camara has escaped with a reprimand despite ignoring "multiple" radio warnings that led to a "clearly dangerous" incident involving Charles Leclerc.

Midway through FP2 at Interlagos, Camara, handed his F1 debut this weekend with Haas, was dawdling on the racing line, climbing the hill in the final sector as Leclerc's Ferrari came through on a flying lap.

Leclerc was squeezed towards the outside wall at high speed, but escaped without damage - although he did make his displeasure at Camara known, with the incident reported to the stewards for an investigation.

After speaking with Camara, team representatives, and reviewing video, team radio and in-car video evidence, the stewards found that "car 51 was warned multiple times that car 16 was arriving on a fast lap.

"Yet, car 51 was weaving and moving well into the racing line. Car 16 had to take evasive action to avoid a collision by moving to the right, with a significant amount of the car off the track.

"The situation that was created was clearly dangerous and car 51 should have taken more care to avoid impeding car 16.

"While the typical penalty for impeding in a Free Practice session is a warning, in this instance, we are of the view that a reprimand is warranted."

title: Kimi Antonelli names major challenge facing every F1 driver at Sao Paulo GP
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has described how the bumps under braking at Turn 1 at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix will be a challenge all weekend.

The world champion finished second and first in the two Friday practice sessions, but the two outings were blighted by drivers running wide after locking up for the first downhill left of the Senna S.

The bumps under braking, coupled with low tyre temperatures, combined to make braking tricky, with laps being instantly ruined if drivers were required to cut across the run-off - which Antonelli did on his first soft tyre lap in FP1.

Reflecting on the situation, the Mercedes driver explained how he was trying to modulate the brake pressure to find the right balance.

"It's quite bumpy [into Turn 1], so it is not easy to find the right braking spot because the grip is coming up and you try to brake later and later," Antonelli said.

"It is quite bumpy, so it is hard to manage brake pressure, so it is not easy, and I was trying to do a little bit more, but it was a bit too much."

Turning to his day overall, Antonelli felt there were still improvements to be made to his W17 on the longer runs.

"I felt good with the car over a single lap, but on the long run, there's a bit of work to do, but overall, I am feeling good and excited for [qualifying].

"I think we have a good chance for [qualifying], however, we're all very close.

"McLaren is strong as well. Red Bull is strong, so we just try our best to be ready. Also, we'll see how the weather is going to be, but I'm really excited.

"The track is a lot of fun. The grip is a bit low, but I'm trying to do my best."

title: Liam Lawson backed for new F1 option if Racing Bulls swing axe
excerpt:
Former F1 driver Martin Brundle has backed Liam Lawson to find a seat on the grid elsewhere if he is dropped by Racing Bulls.

The New Zealander has not yet heard whether he will be retained by the Faenza-based squad for next year despite his impressive run of performances.

Lawson has consistently placed himself in the point-scoring positions this year and sits ninth in the drivers' championship, the leading performer outside of the drivers at the top four teams.

The 24-year-old is facing competition for his seat from F2 title protagonist Nikola Tsolov, who made his FP1 debut with the team in Mexico.

Brundle insisted F1 is a “brutal business” as the wait for Lawson goes on.

“That's very strange, isn't it?” Brundle said, speaking to Sky F1.

“He's done such a great job, he's scored so many points. They're comfortably fifth in the world championship.

“But this is a brutal business, and you get a chance to drive an F1 car because somebody else has been kicked out.”

Regardless of what decision is made regarding Lawson, Brundle is adamant it will not spell the end of his F1 career.

“Watching Esteban [Ocon]'s name come down [in Mexico], it did seem like the front of a bus or the front of a train changing names quite frequently. It's very unusual these days.

“But Liam has done enough to stay in F1. If he's not got that job, he'll either be a super sub, or he'll get a slot quite quickly somewhere else.

“He's been outstanding this year, but it depends on what the team wants to project for the future.”

title: F1 champions trade places as mist descends on Sao Paulo GP practice
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli underlined his new-found status as F1 champion by comfortably setting the fastest lap in a Friday practice for the São Paulo Grand Prix that was blighted by mist.

Free of the burden of bidding for the title, and after recovering from an illness that affected him during last weekend's Mexico City GP in which finishing third was enough to see him crowned as F1's youngest champion, Antonelli was the only driver who managed to dip into the 1:10s for a lap around the renowned Interlagos.

Under a cloud bank that slowly descended over the circuit as the session wore on, and with low track temperatures ahead of a weekend set to be heavily affected by rain, Antonelli posted a time of one minute 10.763s on the soft-compound Pirellis.

It easily pushed McLaren's Lando Norris off top spot by a quarter of a second, and reversed the standings at the end of FP1 when the Briton finished fastest by 0.082s ahead of the 20-year-old.

Max Verstappen, as was the case in FP1, was third quickest in his Red Bull, with the four-time F1 champion, Norris and George Russell in his Mercedes in fourth, separated by just 0.020s.

[Article continues below]

On his first push lap in the opening few minutes of the session, Antonelli posted the third-quickest lap of the day, only bettered by his own and that of the leading time from Norris in FP1, with a 1:11.857s on hard tyres.

The Italian came within three thousandths of a second of that lap on his next outing before the long runs unfolded. At that stage, Norris was second fastest, 0.209s adrift, followed by Verstappen, a further 0.075s down, both on the medium compound.

A trait from FP1 that continued throughout FP2 was the number of drivers needing to use the sizeable run-off area out of Turn 1, heading into the Senna S.

The issue appeared to be a bump on the approach into the downhill left-hander, forcing drivers - including the likes of Antonelli and Russell - off track.

Twenty-five minutes into the session, Russell was the first driver to venture out on the soft tyres, and he immediately went quickest with a time almost eight-tenths faster than Antonelli.

It was a benchmark rapidly wiped out by Norris by 0.020s before Verstappen split the pair, finishing six-thousandths adrift of the outgoing champion.

Antonelli, though, showed his hand soon after, setting the lap that remained unbeaten through to the end of the session.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was fifth quickest, 0.321s adrift, with the Ferraris of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc surprisingly off the pace in sixth and seventh at a track many believed would suit the SF-26s.

Hamilton was 0.450s down and Leclerc, who missed FP1 as reserve Dino Begovic took up the Monégasque's seat, finished 0.720s adrift.

Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, Isack Hadjar in his Red Bull and Haas' Oliver Bearman completed the top 10, the latter 1.228s behind Antonelli.

Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas was the slowest of those who set a time in 21st, finishing 2.620s adrift.

Sadly for Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, he failed to even get into the car due to a terminal issue initially encountered by reserve Freddie Slater in FP1 that restricted the 18-year-old to seven laps.

The stewards only have one investigation to mull over, that involving Haas rookie Rafael Camara, the Brazilian making his F1 debut in front of his home crowd this weekend, but caught heavily impeding Leclerc.

title: Toto Wolff offers first insight into Esteban Ocon axe from Haas
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has offered a glimpse into the difference of opinion that led to Esteban Ocon's axe by Haas over last weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.

Haas confirmed on Saturday morning that Ocon would not drive for the team for the remainder of the weekend.

The decision followed a heated radio exchange during second practice in Mexico, when Ocon contested a call from engineer Laura Mueller to switch his high-fuel run from soft to medium tyres. It is understood the situation escalated in the Friday debrief with team principal Ayao Komatsu, who has refused to go into detail on what was said.

Ryo Hirakawa deputised for Ocon across the remainder of the weekend at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez. After post-race penalties were handed out, the Japanese collected a point for a 10th-place finish.

On Tuesday, Haas announced Ocon would not drive for the team in the remaining four grands prix of the season, bringing his time with Haas to an abrupt end.

For this weekend, Rafael Camara, previously announced as Ocon's replacement for next season, will make his F1 debut in front of his home crowd in the São Paulo Grand Prix.

Wolff, who has known Ocon since his junior career, is the first senior paddock figure to speak publicly about the breakdown, framing it as a clash between Komatsu's need to protect his team and Ocon's conviction that he had done nothing wrong.

Speaking about the situation to the media, including RacingNews365, Mercedes team principal Wolff said Komatsu had been left with no choice but to act.

"At the end it came to the point where Ayao needed to represent the team and protect the team from certain rhetoric," said Wolff.

"On the other side, Esteban felt that personally, he wasn't wrong in the things he said.

"You've got to respect that in the end the team calls the shots. The team principal needs to decide when it's enough, and that is what Ayao did."

[Article continues below]

Wolff details remarkable Vasseur deal for Ocon big break

Wolff's comments carry weight given his long history with Ocon, stretching back to the Frenchman's junior single-seater days. The Austrian explained how Mercedes first took on managing Ocon's career through driver development advisor Gwen Lagrue, before helping fund his route into Formula 1.

"So at Mercedes, we picked up the management of Esteban, due to Gwen," said Wolff. "That's how we got to know Gwen, when Gravity defaulted, and then we agreed to work with Fred [Vasseur] in GP3. We won the championship together.

"Then there wasn't really an opportunity in Formula One. Then the DTM door opened, and we did that together."

Then detailing a remarkable situation between Mercedes and Vasseur that helped give Ocon his F1 break, Wolff said: "I don't know if this is known, when suddenly there appeared to be a free seat at Manor from Spa onwards [2016 Belgian GP], it needed $2 million.

"We said we could provide $1 million for that seat, but we were missing $1 million, and Fred put the money in personally to give Esteban the opportunity.

"Over all those years, I think we were all very supportive and very strong in trying to make sure that Esteban would have the best possible opportunity."

title: Ferrari reveal outcome of crunch Hamilton-Leclerc meeting after Mexico spat
excerpt:
Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur has explained how drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc are now fully aware of their "guidelines" after a crunch meeting in Brazil.

The row between the drivers was sparked by Leclerc's action on the opening lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix, where he attacked around the outside of Hamilton at Turn 4.

Both cars went off the track, with Hamilton delayed just enough to allow Max Verstappen to sneak up the inside to grab second place - behind Leclerc, who was then handed a five-second time penalty by the stewards.

Ultimately, Hamilton felt this action had cost the team a one-two finish, as he said over the radio that the team had "big problems", and then declared post-race he was "really pi**ed" at Leclerc and the situation, whom he said had a "do or die" attitude on-track.

Vasseur then accused both drivers of showing a "lack of respect" to Ferrari in the incident, with the trio holding a crunch meeting on Thursday of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix weekend.

"It went well. It was good to discuss, good to clarify my position and their position," Vasseur told media, including RacingNews365, about the meeting.

"It was good to do, and now we turn the page, and we are focused on the next race.

"The guidelines are still the same. I think they have accumulated perhaps a bit of frustration because they are starting each weekend side-by-side and you have an accumulation effect.

"But at the end of the day, the guidelines are always the same: they need to respect each other. They are two competitors with the fighting spirit for sure, but they need to have respect for the other one.

"But mainly and firstly, they need to respect the brand, the team, the people working at home, the people working on track. I think we are putting in a lot of effort on this, and the message was clear, and will stay clear."

[Article continues below]

Ferrari hold crunch Hamilton-Leclerc talks

When then asked if dealing with the Hamilton-Leclerc dynamic was the most challenging of his career, Vasseur explained that he was prepared to deal with the negatives.

"We have two experienced guys, two competitive guys, and it is now four or five races in a row that we are scoring the highest number of points after Monza and Madrid," he said.

"For sure you have that kind of escalation that you all want to win races, and I think it's probably the downside of the system is that we have two competitive guys starting each weekend next to each other, but I think if we are P2 today [in the constructors'], it's also because we have two guys who are very, very close, and we have to manage it.

"But it's a choice; it's a choice of the lineup. And I have the positive and the negative, but I will deal with the negative."

Vasseur was then pushed on whether the two drivers had agreed to work together for the sake of the team, where he indicated that Ferrari "had failed."

"It is true for every single team that on the grid the drivers are working for the team and the team has to come first," he said.

"For sure, in this situation, we failed collectively because we were one-two, and we didn't win the race in the end.

"That means that it's clear that we failed, and we have to react. But the conclusion of the meeting yesterday evening was clear.

"It was a clear reminder that Ferrari is coming first. It's coming first for the brand, for the employees, for the Tifosi, and we have to keep this in mind."

title: Valtteri Bottas insists Cadillac seat safe despite growing F1 axe rumours
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has insisted he remains relaxed about his Cadillac future, despite mounting speculation that Colton Herta could replace him for 2027.

The Finn, who joined Cadillac for its debut season alongside Sergio Perez, holds a multi-year deal to extend his stay into 2027. That option has yet to be formally triggered by the American outfit, fuelling talk in the paddock that a change could be coming.

Herta, who has been building super licence points through a string of Free Practice 1 outings this season, has emerged as a leading contender for the seat, with Cadillac having made no secret of its ambition to field an American driver.

Following his latest first practice appearance in São Paulo, the American driver does now have the necessary points total to race in F1.

Speaking to select media, including RacingNews365, Bottas admitted he had been taken aback by the scale of the rumours.

"I'm quite surprised about the amount of noise on that because I know what my situation is, and yeah, all I've heard is that the team has been happy with what I'm doing," Bottas said.

"But at the same time, we know how this sport works, and especially now, everyone wants to be in Formula 1, and if somebody sees an opportunity somewhere, they're going to try and go for it, one way or the other.

"But yeah, the way our team is structured and the way decisions are made for the future, everything needs to be approved by the board. And I believe that meeting is still yet to happen. But yeah, I've been convinced that nothing has changed. So that's where we are."

Valtteri Bottas agrees Cadillac axe would be a surprise

Herta is not the only external name being linked to Bottas' cockpit. Mercedes reserve driver Fred Vesti has also been positioning himself as a candidate, having impressed in Mexico by finishing third in Free Practice 1 while standing in for George Russell, just 0.111 seconds behind Kimi Antonelli.

The Dane's ties to General Motors, having raced and won titles for Cadillac in IMSA sports car competition, have only strengthened the chatter.

Asked how odd it would be if Cadillac were to question his performances after a season of following team instructions and utilising his experience, Bottas replied: "I agree. Yeah, it would be very odd. So that's why I don't think anything is going to change with my situation.

"That was kind of always the deal, and all season I've been really following instructions, and sometimes it has been very clear that I should just try and get the car over the finish line.

"But of course, there are always people who look from the outside. They don't maybe understand the big picture, and then you get the criticism, which is normal in the sport.

"But it's just the main thing is that we know where we are. I know that, I know what my job is, and if they want something further from me, then I'm sure they will tell me."

title: Dan Ticktum fronts Fortescue Formula E launch amid Taylor Barnard legal battle
excerpt:
Fortescue Zero Racing officially launched on Thursday, revealing its livery at Shoreditch Electric Light Station in London ahead of its maiden Formula E campaign.

The British-based, Australian-licensed outfit was formed through Fortescue's acquisition of Penske Autosport and will compete under Gen4 regulations from the 2026/27 season, running Jaguar customer powertrains out of its Kidlington base.

Dr Andrew Forrest, Fortescue's founder and executive chairman, attended the launch alongside company CEO and former Argentina rugby captain Gus Pichot.

Also present were Claire Williams, who serves as a global brand ambassador for Fortescue Zero without holding an operational role at the team, and team principal Jim Wright, whose background spans senior roles at Williams, Toro Rosso and Virgin Racing in Formula 1 before a decade embedded in Formula E leadership with Mahindra, Venturi and Andretti.

"We’re not here to blend in. We’re here to build a team that competes, does things differently and

earns its place on the grid," said Wright.

"This is the world’s first look at who we are. But the real work is well underway, to be ready, push

hard and deliver as a team when we begin running on-circuit next week.

"Launching a new racing outfit is a significant challenge, and that’s exactly what makes it exciting.

We have strong foundations, an experienced, talented and highly motivated group and we’re

ready to compete."

Dan Ticktum, confirmed as one half of the team's debut driver line-up, was also in attendance. The Briton joins from Cupra Kiro, where his exit followed internal friction over disciplinary and contractual matters.

RacingNews365 attended Fortescue Zero's first Formula E launch, with it unveiling an exciting black and green livery for the upcoming campaign. The livery contains hidden details of Fortescue's birth, what it believes in and where it is heading, including nods to Dr Forrest and Sir Frank Williams.

Crucially, the team's other driver, Taylor Barnard, was not in attendance.

Taylor Barnard absence a notable launch factor

Taylor Barnard, the other driver signed to partner Ticktum, was notably absent from proceedings.

According to Formula E Notebook, His management company, PHM Racing Academy, has lodged a legal challenge seeking to void his Fortescue Zero contract, aiming to free the driver to explore other options for the Gen4 debut season.

Fortescue Zero maintains that Barnard remains contractually bound to the team, but the dispute meant the driver skipped the launch entirely.

It remains unclear whether the legal challenge will succeed or whether Barnard will ultimately line up for the team when testing gets underway in just over a week.
